title: Correcting Your Leader Is Best Done by Asking for Clarity Instead
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the delicate task of giving upward feedback when a leader has made a visible mistake. Because direct correction risks embarrassment or a defensive reaction, the author recommends a more indirect approach: asking genuine clarifying questions ('What am I missing?', 'Can you help me understand what occurred?') that let the leader arrive at the realization themselves. This framing, presented as curiosity rather than accusation, reduces the odds of confrontation while still surfacing the mistake for correction. The piece closes with a martial-arts analogy about the value of subtlety over direct confrontation with a powerful adversary.
points: Correcting a leader directly risks embarrassment and defensive reactions.
Asking clarifying questions lets a leader reach the realization of their own mistake without confrontation.
Effective clarifying questions position the team member as a learner rather than a critic.
This indirect approach reduces risk to the team member's credibility with the leader.
The article compares this approach to a martial-arts principle of subtlety over head-on confrontation.
quotes: When the leader above you makes a mistake, says the wrong thing in a group or client setting, or grossly misreads a situation, it is imperative that they understand the potential consequences and stand ready to make a correction.
Leaders can sometimes overreact to being corrected, as they often find it embarrassing or as a sign they are being disrespected.
One avenue is not to correct the leader or point out the blunder, but to ask them to clarify instead.

Presuming the leader has a reason or logic behind what they did, asking them to clarify and help you learn through the explanation will often unearth the truth that indeed a mistake was made that needs to be corrected.
Correcting your leader can sometimes be risky. Getting curious and taking the more indirect path to raise the issue is often the best call.
As any martial arts master will tell you, the strongest move isn’t always engaging your opponent head-on.
